newsitem.title: USA: U.S. firms attack Japan for currency manipulation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. firms attack Japan for currency manipulation.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
American manufacturing companies Tuesday accused Japan of manipulating currency markets for its own ends and warned that the result will be slower economic growth in the United States.
"The Japanese, and to some extent the Europeans ... seem to be looking to export away their problems," National Association of Manufacturers President Jerry Jasinowski said.

He told a conference sponsored by the Economic Strategy Institute think tank that Tokyo had deliberately engineered a steep drop in its currency against the dollar to boost the competitiveness of Japanese products on world markets.

Jasinowski and others at the conference called on the Clinton administration to take Japan to task for its alleged currency manipulation. But there was no sign that the administration, which has consistently held to a strong dollar policy over the past two years, was listening.

"Exchange rate developments in the last few months are cause for concern," Jasinowski said. "The current level of the dollar is preventing the expected boom in U.S. exports." A stronger dollar tends to make U.S. exports less competitive.

Michael Farren, a vice president at Xerox Corp. and a former U.S. trade official, echoed Jasinowski's remarks about Japan's alleged currency manipulation. "This has been very much a yen problem, not a dollar problem," he said.

The dollar has risen some 40 percent against the yen since hitting a record low of 79.75 yen in April of last year, pushed up by buying by Japan's central bank, the Bank of Japam, and to a lesser extent, the United States itself.

The dollar briefly approached 115 yen earlier this month, before falling back on suggestions by a senior Japanese official that its rise against the yen might be about to end. The dollar stood at 111.65 yen in New York Tuesday, up slightly from Monday's level.
But Lawrence Chimerine, chief economist at the institute, warned the United States against being fooled by such comments.

He suggested that Tokyo may have temporarily talked the dollar down ahead of a meeting this month between President Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Manila on the fringes of a gathering of Asia Pacific leaders.

Saying the United States had acquiesced to the dollar's rise against the yen, Chimerine called for an end to that policy and said Washington should tell Tokyo that it will no longer accept deliberate manipulation of currency rates.
"The U.S. government should maybe take a more interventionist view to exchange rate management," added University of Maryland Professor Peter Morici.

Morici argued that economic growth will slow next year to 1.5 percent to 2 percent if something is not done to bring down the dollar against the yen and lower domestic interest rates. Growth this year is expected to be about 2.5 percent.

Jasinowski agreed that an overvalued dollar carried risks. "If the current expansion is to continue, everything possible must be done to increase exports by not letting our trading partners prop up the dollar," he said.
He saw "downside risks" for the U.S. economy next year, with growth slowing to the "two percent range".

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin last week reiterated the administration's support for a strong dollar, saying it was in America's interests, and rejected suggestions that Washington use the currency as a trade tool for competitive advantage.
Although some administration officials privately questioned that view, they admitted that Rubin and the Treasury remain firmly in control of U.S. dollar policy.
The strong dollar helps the United States by holding down the price of imports, inflation and interest rates.

Rubin believes that economic fundamentals ultimately determine currency rates and is not enamored with attempts to micro-manage the currency market. That is why he is careful to speak out in favor of a strong, not a stronger, dollar.
The Treasury chief though has also made no secret of the need for Japan to pursue policies to boost domestic demand and not rely on a cheap yen to export its way out of a sluggish economy.
Some U.S. officials have recently been concerned by signs of slowing Japanese growth after a surge earlier in the year.
